title: Production Incident: Statement Timeout vs Lock Timeout Cascading Outage
realWorldScenario: To prevent slow queries from hanging the database, an engineer set `statement_timeout = '5s'` globally. Later, a background migration ran `ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN flags INT;`. The DDL failed after 5 seconds, but during those 5 seconds, the entire payment API experienced an outage.
questionStatement: Explain how PostgreSQL lock queues work and why a waiting DDL statement holding an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock request blocks all subsequent read and write queries. Why did `statement_timeout` fail to prevent the outage, and how does `lock_timeout` eliminate cascading lock pileups?

symptoms: Hundreds of client HTTP requests timed out
DDL command aborted with statement timeout
Normal fast 2ms SELECT queries queued up and failed
candidateTasks: Explain why lock requests form a FIFO queue where exclusive locks block subsequent reads
Demonstrate the safe DDL execution pattern using lock_timeout and retry loops

expectedConcepts: FIFO lock queue mechanics and exclusive lock blocking subsequent reads
Difference between statement_timeout (execution + lock) and lock_timeout (lock wait only)
Why waiting DDL starves all incoming traffic
Safe DDL pattern setting lock_timeout = 500ms with retry loops
Preventing API connection exhaustion during schema maintenance
hints: Why do new SELECT queries wait behind a waiting ALTER TABLE in PostgreSQL?
statement_timeout includes time spent waiting for locks.
What happens if lock_timeout is set to 200 milliseconds?
